label: Troops Withdrawn Before Election Day
detail: Federal soldiers leave South Carolina, Florida and Louisiana months before the vote, so Black voters there face local white militias and rifle clubs without federal protection.
assumption: With no federal garrisons, intimidation of Black voters rises and their turnout falls in the three states, and the Black voters who do turn out vote as they did in 1876. White turnout and vote choice stay as observed.
facts_text: By order of the President, federal troops were withdrawn from South Carolina, Florida and Louisiana in the spring and summer of 1876, and none remain at the statehouses or in the country districts.
Armed white clubs have drilled openly in these states, and Black citizens have been warned of what will follow if they go to the polls.
research_questions: How far did Black turnout fall in South Carolina, Louisiana and Florida where armed white clubs operated and federal troops were absent?
How did Black voters in the Deep South vote and turn out in places where troops had already left, such as Mississippi in 1875?
How did white turnout change in these states when intimidation was open and federal enforcement was weak?
source_text: Federal troops are withdrawn from South Carolina, Florida and Louisiana months before the 1876 election.
